titulo: George Müller · Father to the orphans

guion.texto: Bristol, March 1898. The blinds are drawn, the flags fly at half-mast, and tens of thousands of people fill the streets to say goodbye to an old man who, when he died, owned little more than his books and some furniture. For more than sixty years he had cared for thousands of orphans without asking anyone for money. His story begins far from here, in Prussia, with a boy who stole.
George Müller was born on September 27, 1805, in Kroppenstedt, in the kingdom of Prussia. His father was a tax collector.
Before he was ten years old, George was already stealing the government money his father kept at home.
One day his father counted out a sum of money, left it in plain sight… and waited.
Some money is missing, George.
They found it hidden in the boy’s shoe.
His father wanted him to become a clergyman so that he would have a good living, and sent him to study at the cathedral school in Halberstadt.
In 1820, when George was 14, his mother died.
That night he was playing cards until two in the morning. The next day he went to a tavern.
At 16 he ran away with money he had collected for his father. He stayed in expensive hotels, left his best clothes as security and tried to leave an inn without paying.
He was taken to prison. The cell was narrow, with a small window of thick iron bars. At night he heard the bolts and the keys. He was given very coarse bread and water.
I now found myself, at the age of sixteen, an inmate of the same dwelling with thieves and murderers, and treated accordingly.
To pass the time he asked for a Bible. They did not give him one.
He was held from December 18 until January 12. His father paid what he owed… and then punished him severely.
At the school in Nordhausen he got up at four in the morning and studied until ten at night. On his walks he spoke Latin with the director.
But he kept running into debt, and even faked a robbery to deceive his creditors.
I had about three hundred books of my own, but no Bible.
At Easter 1825 he began studying theology at the university of Halle. Soon he had pawned his watch and even his clothes.
There he met Beta, an old schoolmate. With him and other students he travelled for 43 days to Switzerland, using passports obtained with letters from their parents that George forged.
One Saturday in November, Beta told him he was going to a meeting in a house, where they read the Bible, prayed and sang.
No sooner had I heard this, than it was to me as if I had found something after which I had been seeking all my life long.
The meeting was at the house of Mr. Wagner, a believing tradesman.
Come as often as you please; house and heart are open to you.
They sang a hymn. Then a student named Kayser knelt down and prayed.
This kneeling down made a deep impression upon me; for I had never either seen any one on his knees, nor had I ever prayed myself on my knees.
They read a chapter of the Bible and a printed sermon, because in Prussia it was not allowed to expound the Scriptures without an ordained clergyman. At the end the man of the house prayed.
All we have seen on our journey to Switzerland, and all our former pleasures, are as nothing in comparison with this evening.
Years later he would write:
That evening was the turning point in my life.

He went back to Wagner’s house on the Sunday, the Monday and many times more. He left the taverns, his bad companions and the habit of lying. He even burned the manuscript of a novel he was translating to pay for a trip to Paris.
In Halle he saw many times the great orphanage founded by August Hermann Francke. That sight stayed with him.
In March 1829 he arrived in London to train as a missionary to the Jews. He studied about twelve hours a day, mostly Hebrew, until he fell ill.
He went to Teignmouth, on the Devon coast, to recover. There he met Henry Craik, a Scot and a Hebrew scholar. They would be friends and fellow workers for 36 years.
From then on, he wrote, he was “a lover of the Word of God.” Early in 1830 he stayed on as minister of the small Ebenezer Chapel in Teignmouth.
On October 7, 1830, he married Mary Groves, sister of the missionary Anthony Norris Groves.
That same month he gave up his fixed salary. He ended the renting of pews and put a box in the chapel for anyone who wished to give.
Mary and he sold their possessions and decided to ask no one for anything: only the Lord.
“Sell your possessions and give to the poor. Provide yourselves with purses that will not wear out, an inexhaustible treasure in heaven” (Luke 12:33 · BSB)
On November 18, 1830, they had about eight shillings left.
They prayed.
Four hours later, a sister came to him.
I told the brethren, dear sister, when I gave up my salary, that I would for the future tell the Lord only about my wants.
But He has told me to give you some money.
She gave him two guineas.
In April 1832 Müller and Craik preached in Bristol.
I feel that Bristol is my place for a while. The Lord mercifully teach me!
They arrived with their families on May 25, and at first the two families lived together in a house of six rooms.
In July cholera reached Bristol. Müller and Craik visited the sick. For about four months there were prayer meetings every morning, from six to eight, with two or three hundred people.
They took Bethesda Chapel only on condition of not going into debt.
On August 13, on the front bench, seven believers began a church there. The first to join was Mary.

This evening one brother and four sisters united with brother Craik and me in church fellowship at Bethesda, without any rules, desiring only to act as the Lord shall be pleased to give us light through His Word.
In September their daughter Lydia was born.
Müller remembered the poor neglected children he had seen running about the streets at Teignmouth.
On November 20, 1835, he came across a biography of Francke. The next day he decided to set to work on an orphan house.
He wanted it to be seen that God is faithful still and hears prayer still: the orphans would receive all they needed only by prayer and faith, without asking anyone.
On December 2 he told Craik about it, and Craik encouraged him.
On December 5 he read in the Psalms:
“Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it.” (Psalm 81:10 · BSB)
I fell on my knees, and asked the Lord for premises, for £1,000, and for suitable individuals to take care of the children.
On December 9 he held a public meeting. On purpose, there was no collection. Even so he was given ten shillings, and a sister offered herself for the work.
That same day the first piece of furniture arrived: a large wardrobe. Then came plates, jugs, blankets and cloth.
A poor seamstress, who earned about three and a half shillings a week, brought a hundred pounds.
The Lord Jesus has given His last drop of blood for me, and should I not give Him this £100?
The day set for receiving applications for children came… and none came.
Müller spent the evening in prayer.
I could say from my heart, that I should rejoice in God being glorified in this matter, though it were by bringing the whole to nothing.
The very next day, February 4, the first application came.
In April the first home opened at number 6 Wilson Street, furnished for 30 girls. By May, 26 girls aged seven to twelve lived there.
Now we have a home!
That same year another home opened for the youngest. In June 1837 the thousand pounds he had asked for were complete, without his having asked any person for anything.
“A father of the fatherless and a defender of widows is God in His holy habitation.” (Psalm 68:5 · BSB)
From 1838 came hard years. There were days when the money was enough only for that day’s food. Müller wrote down every need, every gift and every answer.
In September 1838 he gathered his fellow workers. He asked that the children should lack nothing in food or clothing:
I would rather at once send them away than that they should lack.
And they made a rule: never to buy anything except they could pay for it at once, however much it might seem to be needed.
So much prayer, and so little coming in, I never knew.
Neither the children nor any other person can have perceived our poverty.
In the spring of 1841 he learned something he would keep for the rest of his life: to begin each day meditating on the Word before praying.
I saw more clearly than ever, that the first great and primary business to which I ought to attend every day was, to have my soul happy in the Lord.
In 1845 a neighbour on Wilson Street complained, courteously, about the children’s noise.

This complaint is neither without foundation, nor unjust. I should myself feel it trying to my head to live next door to the Orphan Houses, on that account. I therefore ought to do to others, as I should wish to be done by.
He decided to build. Mary and he prayed together every morning for the building. In February 1846 he found a field of nearly seven acres on Ashley Down.
The owner told him he had lain awake that night thinking about it, and sold it to him at £120 an acre instead of £200. The architect offered the plans for free.
In July 1846 came the largest gift so far: £2,050.
I was neither excited nor surprised; for I look out for answers to my prayers. I believe that God hears me.
That same month, while he was praying about four needs, a gentleman from Devonshire arrived and gave him twenty pounds to be divided among the four.
Thus I received, at the very moment that I had been asking God, four answers to my prayers.
I am as certain that this house of mercy will be built, as if it were already standing before me.
Between June 18 and 21, 1849, the children moved from Wilson Street into the first house on Ashley Down, built for 300.
It was a great, plain building of grey stone, with hundreds of windows. A few days later, Müller wrote:
There is already such a measure of order established in the house, by the help of God, as that things can be done by the minute hands of the time pieces.
The children got up at six. Until breakfast, the girls knitted and the boys read.
At eight they had oatmeal porridge with milk for breakfast. Then came a short service, school, play and work in the gardens.
The girls wore green checked cloaks and straw bonnets; the boys, navy blue jackets and caps.
On Sundays they walked in line to Bethesda. And every September 27 they celebrated Müller’s birthday.
Then came more houses: in 1857, 1862, 1868 and 1870. When the fifth was finished, Ashley Down had room for 2,050 orphans.
In January 1866 Henry Craik died, after seven months of illness.
My beloved fellow-labourer and intimate friend for thirty-six years.
Mary had worked 34 years in the work “with a motherly love.” In February 1870 she had been in bed for six days.
My darling, I am sorry to have to leave you, but I shall return as soon as I can.
You leave me with Jesus.
The next day, when George told her that Jesus was coming for her, she answered:
He will soon come.
She died on February 6, 1870, after 39 years of marriage.
About 1,200 of the orphans who were able to walk followed the procession. George himself preached at the funeral, on this verse:
“You are good, and You do what is good; teach me Your statutes.” (Psalm 119:68 · BSB)
For years Mary had walked home with him from the orphan houses every night. Now he went back alone.
I shall not meet my beloved wife at home, but I shall meet the Lord Jesus, my precious Friend; He will comfort me.
In November 1871 he married Susannah Grace Sangar, whom he had known for more than 25 years.
In 1875, at 69, he began travelling to preach. Until 1892 he covered some 200,000 miles across Europe, America, Asia, Australia and Africa.
Susannah always went with him. She did not speak in public: she handed out tracts and Bibles in many languages and talked with people.
Susannah died in 1894. George kept reading the Bible every morning; he had read it through, he said, more than a hundred times. In 1897 he wrote:
I have been for sixty-eight years and three months, viz., since July, 1829, a lover of the Word of God, and that uninterruptedly.
I am a very, very happy man.
When someone told him he would enter heaven like a ship in full sail, he answered:
Oh, no; it is poor George Müller, who needs daily to pray, Hold Thou me up that my footsteps slip not.
On Wednesday, March 9, 1898, he led the prayer meeting of the house. The next morning he was found dead in his room, beside his bed. He was 92.

He was buried in Arnos Vale cemetery, under a yew tree, beside Mary and Susannah. When he died he left about £160: his books, some furniture and a little money. Nearly one and a half million pounds had passed through his hands, all given without his asking, and in his lifetime he cared for more than ten thousand orphans. He did not want to be remembered himself, but for it to be seen that God is faithful still and hears prayer still.
“A father of the fatherless and a defender of widows is God in His holy habitation.” (Psalm 68:5 · BSB)

Sources: the autobiography of George Müller (G. F. Bergin’s edition, 1905) and A. T. Pierson’s biography (1899). The girl on Wilson Street and the children of Ashley Down stand for the real orphans; their names are not recorded.
